name: Flexible conductor
summary: A wavy conductor line showing a connection that must flex, such as a lead to moving equipment or a vibration break.
description: The flexible conductor mark replaces a straight run of conductor with a wave or loop to show that the connection is intended to bend in service. Typical uses are leads to hinged doors, pendant control stations, crane festoons, motor terminal boxes on resilient mounts and short links that absorb thermal movement between busbars and equipment.

On a schematic the wave says nothing about the cable construction. Stranding class, insulation type, bending radius and the number of operating cycles must come from the cable schedule or equipment specification. A drafter should not use the wave simply to make a long wire look tidy, because a reader will assume a moving or vibrating part exists at that point.
readingNotes: Look for the moving or vibrating item at one end of the wavy section.
Check the cable schedule for a flexible stranding class and any drag-chain or festoon rating.
drawingChecklist: Identify the moving part the flexible section serves.
Reference a cable type suited to repeated flexing.
Show strain relief or termination details where the lead leaves the moving part.
distinction: A flexible conductor bends in service; a twisted-pair mark shows conductors twisted together for noise rejection and implies nothing about movement.
